newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lacroix storms catwalk with ethnic patchwork.
newsitem.headline: Lacroix storms catwalk with ethnic patchwork.

text.p: - Forever true to his flamboyant instincts, Christian Lacroix unleashed a collage of African, Indian and 18th-century French inspiration in his ready-to-wear collection on Thursday.

Lacroix's world is one of vivid ethnic and historical references -- lace-up bustiers on checkered kneepants, Marquis jackets with jewelled buttons, swelling Masai princess skirts or bou-bous that hung amply from a band above the breasts.
Each oufit was a wild patchwork, juxtaposing macrame, beads, gold embroidery and bits of lace and luscious shantung.
He stamped a coral suede slip dress with oriental medallions, belted ribbon silk kimonos with ornamental belts, and ringed wedding cake gowns with bands of white ruffles.
"It's everything from Africa to India, but mixed and matched in a way that's for the next millennium," was how Lacroix defined his inspiration. "A city-dweller's exoticism," he added.

Lacroix, whose sales doubled last year, has reason to hope he will finally turn a profit and placate his boss, Bernard Arnault, chairman of luxury goods giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton, when his house marks its 10th anniversary next year.
To help boost revenus, Lacroix is set to launch a line of dinner ware and possibly a new perfume by late 1997.
All eyes this season are on LVMH which is expected to announce next Tuesday the appointment of Britain's mad romantic John Galliano as the new designer for Christian Dior.

Another Briton, the angry and irreverent Alexander McQueen, is tipped for the position Galliano would be leaving vacant at LVMH sister house Givenchy. A brief appearance by McQueen backstage after Lacroix's show was a strong indication he would be Givenchy's new man.
"I really enjoyed it, it's a totally different concept than what I'm all about, but the colours are fantastic," he said.
Asked whether he had decided to accept the Givenchy job, McQueen replied: "I'm afraid you'll have to wait for that."
The breasts and knickers showing through Rifat Ozbek's more than 100 transparent black dresses confirmed this season's trend of nudity and suggestion.

Ozbek's only concession to colour was the mercurochrome red of the models' cheeks and their strings of fake pearls. The emergence on Kate Moss's arm of a man wearing a Union Jack cape seemed contrived in the midst of this monotonous harem.
When, and if, Brazilian designer Ocimar Versolato ever reaches the end of his soul-searching, Paris may well have a virtuoso clothing designer on its hands.
Until then, the fashion community will have to bear with off-key notes alternating with erratic moments of brilliance.
His signature line on Wednesday night was an example.

From unremarkable, slinky rayon knit dresses and sandals buckling heavily up the calf, Versolato switched to the Japanese influence of a striking magenta satin wrap-around mini with kimono collar, or a liquid, wing-sleeved lavender bolero.
Then he jolted to grey wool toile suits, intricately cut but not as razor-sharp as he is capable of, and a violet sheath with gaping sideseams over five-and-dime panties.

There were some magical sparks -- a draped column of bronze chiffon, a slate grey mikado bustier gown sashed with copper silk. Beautifully crafted little black cocktail dresses emanated that fragile sexuality Versolato endeavours to portray.
"He has taken major strides," said Joan Kaner of Neiman Marcus department stores. "I loved the kimono effects, the irridescent chiffons. There was a beautiful mastery of draping."

Versolato has been watched very closely since being named ready-to-wear designer at Lanvin barely a year ago. His first show for the house last March was panned by the fashion press, and his second chance comes on Saturday.
